vignette:
The Audition

Maya sits in the waiting room of her agent's office, script in hand, running lines silently. She's been doing this for fifteen years-the preparation, the waiting, the careful cultivation of different versions of herself. At thirty-five, she's landed steady work in television and theater, enough to pay rent in the city and maintain the life she's built. But lately, even the familiar rhythm of auditions feels different, colored by something she can't quite name.

The trauma that changed everything happened two years ago on a film set in New Mexico. Maya was between takes, standing near the equipment trucks, when a grip named David suffered a catastrophic fall from a rigging platform. She watched it happen in real time-the slip, the terrible silence as his body fell, the sound when he hit the ground. She held his hand while the paramedics worked. She rode in the ambulance. She waited in the hospital while his family arrived. David survived, but with severe spinal injuries that left him partially paralyzed.

For months afterward, Maya told herself she was fine. She wasn't the one injured. She had a job to do-finishing the film, moving on to the next project. But somewhere in the months that followed, something fractured inside her.

Now, when she auditions, Maya finds herself unable to fully inhabit a character the way she used to. She'll be reading a scene, and suddenly she's hyperaware of her body in space-where the nearest exit is, whether there are unstable objects nearby, whether anyone around her looks unsteady. During a callback for a drama series last month, the director asked her to do the scene again, with more vulnerability. Maya froze. She couldn't access that openness. All she could think about was how exposed she felt, how quickly things could go wrong.

Her sleep has become unpredictable. Most nights, she lies awake replaying the moment of the fall, her mind generating variations-what if she'd been standing closer, what if she'd called out a warning, what if she'd caught him somehow. On the nights she does sleep, she wakes gasping, her sheets soaked with sweat. She's stopped accepting evening auditions because she's exhausted by morning.

The hypervigilance has begun to bleed into her daily life. She avoids sets with heights or complex rigging. She's turned down three good roles because of this. Her agent is beginning to ask questions about her availability. Maya hasn't told anyone what happened-not really. When people ask why she's being more selective, she says she's looking for better material, more challenging parts. It's partially true.

What troubles her most is that acting, which has always been her refuge and her identity, now feels unsafe. The collaborative nature of theater and film-the trust required to work with others, to be vulnerable in front of a crew, to depend on technical support systems-all of it now carries an undercurrent of dread. She finds herself watching other people's movements obsessively, assessing risk, waiting for the next disaster.

She's started having panic attacks in crowded spaces-something that never happened before. Last week, she left an audition halfway through because her chest tightened and she couldn't breathe. The casting director looked confused. Maya left without explanation.

She knows something is wrong. She knows she's not herself. But she's also afraid that if she stops working, stops pushing forward, she'll have to actually feel what happened. Right now, staying busy feels like the only thing keeping her afloat.
